transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's a lot of things, really, but the thing that finally made me make the appointment—and keep it, because I've canceled twice before—is that my eating has just gotten so completely off track. I mean, I work as a healthcare support worker, so I'm on my feet constantly, moving patients, running back and forth, and you need energy for that. You really do. But lately, some days I barely get down a cup of coffee and maybe a stale granola bar before a twelve-hour shift. I just look at food and I feel... nothing. Or worse, I just feel too exhausted to even chew. And it's starting to really show. I noticed it last week when I was getting dressed for work. My scrubs, the ones I've worn for two years, they've been hanging so loose on me. I had to pull the drawstring tight just to keep the pants up. And I'm not trying to lose weight at all. I haven't been to a gym in months, I haven't changed my diet on purpose, but the weight is just falling off because I simply cannot bring myself to eat a proper meal. My sister even said something on Sunday when she came over to drop off some mail, she said my face looked hollow, which really bothered me because I try to keep up appearances, you know? But I just can't seem to force myself to eat when my stomach feels like it's tied in a knot of lead.
Are you avoiding food because you fear gaining weight or because of concerns about your body shape?

No, no, it's nothing like that. I really don't care about my body shape or gaining weight. I mean, I'm a 46-year-old guy, I'm not trying to be on a magazine cover or anything. Like I said, I need the energy for my job. I want to eat, I really do. I know I should eat. It's just... the thought of it, the actual process of making food, sitting down, chewing it, swallowing it... it just feels like climbing a mountain. I look at a sandwich and I just feel this heavy, empty exhaustion. It's not about the calories or worrying I'll get fat. If anything, I'd love to put a few pounds back on so my sister stops looking at me like I'm a ghost, and so my scrubs fit right again. I used to enjoy food, you know? I'd make a big pot of chili on my days off, or grill a steak. But now, it's just... there's no desire. It's just a complete lack of appetite, not a fear of food.
Have you been feeling persistently depressed or down most of the day lately?

Yeah... yeah, I have. It's just this constant, inescapable weight. I mean, most mornings I wake up and before my eyes are even fully open, I just get hit with this... this heavy, hollow feeling. It's like the whole day is already completely ruined before I even get out of bed, let alone before I even put on my badge for work. 

My badge sits right there on the nightstand next to my keys and my wallet, exactly where I leave it every night, and I just stare at it and feel so incredibly defeated. I drag myself up, and that heavy feeling, it doesn't wash off in the shower, it doesn't go away when I'm waiting for the bus in the cold... it just sits right in the middle of my chest. All day long. I'll be at work, walking down the linoleum corridors, taking blood pressure or helping someone to the bathroom, and I just feel so profoundly down, almost like I'm moving underwater. 

It's not just a passing sadness, you know? It's not like being upset because you had a bad day or got some bad news. It's like this dark, suffocating blanket that settles over me the exact second I wake up and just follows me through every single hour of my shift. I try to put on a brave face for the patients, I really do, because they're going through their own terrible things and they don't need to see me looking miserable, but inside, I just feel completely empty and sad from morning until I finally go back to sleep. It just never really lifts.
How long have you been feeling this persistently depressed?

Well, it's... it's been a long time. It feels like forever, honestly, but if I really think about it, try to pin it down... it's been about a year and four months of this. This steady, heavy depression. I remember because it was right around the time the leaves started changing last autumn—well, the autumn before last, I guess. I used to love that time of year, you know? Taking walks, feeling the crisp air. But that year, I just didn't care. The leaves changed, and I just felt nothing but this awful weight.

And it wasn't just the depression, it was the loss of interest in everything, too. Like the chili I mentioned earlier—I just stopped wanting to make it. I stopped wanting to do much of anything, really. It just sort of settled in over me, like dust on furniture in a closed-up room, and it hasn't left since. So yeah, roughly a year and four months of just waking up every single day feeling like I'm already defeated before my feet even hit the floor. It's just been this constant companion, this shadow that never, ever leaves my side, no matter what I do or where I go. I go to work, it's there. I come home, it's there. It's just... it's been a very long sixteen months, doctor. Very long.
Have you had thoughts that you would be better off dead or thoughts of hurting yourself?

I... I wouldn't say I want to hurt myself. I haven't, you know, sat down and made a plan or figured out a way to do it. I don't have a specific method in mind or anything like that. I know some people do, they figure out exactly how they're going to end it, but I haven't done that. I couldn't do that to my sister, for one thing. The thought of her getting that phone call, or worse, finding me... no, I haven't planned anything. 

But... it's more like this passive sort of wish, I guess you could call it. It happens a lot, especially at night when I'm lying in bed, staring at the ceiling, dreading the alarm clock going off. I just catch myself thinking, you know, what if I just didn't wake up? What if my heart just quietly stopped in my sleep? It wouldn't be violent, it wouldn't be a mess for anyone to clean up, it would just be... over. The heavy feeling would be gone. 

Or sometimes when I'm waiting for the bus in the morning, and the exhaust from the cars is freezing in the air, I just look at the traffic and think... it would just be so much easier if I could just disappear. Just fade out, like a radio station losing its signal. Not die, necessarily, just... cease to exist. Because existing right now, carrying this weight around every single day, trying to smile at the patients while I feel like I'm crumbling inside... it's just so exhausting. It's so tiring. So yeah, no plans to actually do anything to myself, but the thought of just... not being here anymore, of not having to wake up to this feeling again... that thought is there a lot. It's almost comforting in a weird, messed up way, just imagining the relief of not having to try anymore.
Have you been having trouble concentrating or making decisions lately?

Concentrating? Making decisions? Honestly, no, not really. I mean, I know some people get really scatterbrained when they're down, they can't focus on a book or a TV show, or they stand in the grocery aisle for twenty minutes trying to pick a brand of cereal. But for me, it hasn't really been like that. 

I go to work, and I can still follow the routines. I know exactly what rooms need supplies restocked, I know the protocols for taking vitals, I know how to log the information in the charts without making mistakes. My mind doesn't wander off when I'm listening to a patient tell me about their grandchildren or when the charge nurse is giving instructions for the shift. I hear them, I understand what needs to be done, and I do it. And when I'm home, if I actually force myself to sit and watch a documentary or something, I can follow the plot just fine. I don't lose the thread of it. 

And decisions... well, I don't have a lot of big decisions to make right now anyway, but the day-to-day stuff isn't any harder than usual. I can decide what bus to catch, I can decide what uniform scrubs to wear, even if I don't care how I look in them. It's not that my brain is foggy or confused, it's just... it's just heavy. The machinery up there is still working, the gears are still turning and I can focus on the task at hand, it's just that the engine running it all is completely out of gas. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm having trouble concentrating or deciding things. It's just the awful mood that sits over everything I'm focusing on.
Have you noticed any change in your sleep recently?

Sleep? Oh, my sleep is just... it's a mess. It really is. I used to be the kind of guy who could hit the pillow and be out cold until the alarm went off, you know? Just a solid eight hours, no problem. But now, lately, it’s just completely broken up. I get into bed, usually around ten-thirty or eleven, hoping I'll just crash because I'm so exhausted from the day, but my brain just won't shut off. I just lie there, staring at the ceiling in the dark, and I start replaying everything that happened at work. I'll think about a patient who was upset, or if I stocked the supply cart right, or if the charge nurse looked at me funny... just going over and over these tiny details that I know don't really matter, but I can't stop. 

And then, while I'm doing that, I'm also just... listening. It's so quiet in my apartment at night, but I find myself straining to hear every little creak or groan the building makes. The pipes clanking, a car driving by outside, the wind against the window... I just lie there wide awake, listening to all of it, feeling this sort of low-level hum of anxiety. It takes me forever to finally drift off. 

And even when I do finally fall asleep, it never lasts. It's like clockwork, doctor. I wake up, almost every single night, right around three or four in the morning. My eyes just snap open. And once I'm awake at that hour, that's it. It's game over. I try to settle back down, I flip the pillow over to the cool side, I try taking deep breaths, I try counting backward from a hundred, I try everything. But I just can't get back to sleep. My mind starts racing again, the heavy feeling settles right back into my chest, and I just lie there in the dark for hours, watching the red numbers on the digital clock change, just waiting and waiting for the alarm to finally go off at six. It's agonizing, really, just lying there trapped with my own thoughts, knowing I have to get up and face another day feeling so incredibly tired. It just drains whatever little energy I might have had left. So yeah, my sleep has changed a lot. It's just fragmented and frustrating and... well, it's not really resting at all.
